title: Inflation ‘everywhere’ as profit growth slows
full_text:
Australia’s corporate profit season wrapping up on Monday tells a story of resilience without much excitement and the return of interest rate anxiety.
While 2026 financial year profit growth of 11.6 per cent is solid by historical standards, it’s just 5.3 per cent excluding the contribution of mining and energy. That is a “dismal recovery” after three years of contraction, according to MST senior analyst Hasan Tevfik.
Profit growth is expected to slow to 7.6 per cent in FY27 and 7.3 per cent in FY28. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 is expected to record three straight years of double-digit growth, including 33 per cent this calendar year, due to its deep exposure to the artificial intelligence capex boom.
“The negative is that the improvement is narrowly based,” said AMP deputy chief economist Diana Mousina.
Healthcare names such as CSL and Cochlear stood out, along with Super Retail Group, Universal Store, Mirvac and REA, but these were cases of “less bad than feared” rather than genuine strength. News Corp, the publisher of The Australian, is the biggest shareholder of REA. Only 36 per cent of companies beat expectations, below the usual 40 per cent, while 59 per cent lifted dividends from a year ago.
Tevfik flags a relatively sharp 2.7 per cent cut to the consensus FY27 profit forecast to $159bn, much of it currency related. Commodity earnings have been cut by 4.4 per cent as costs climb even as sales forecast lift. And industrials are getting help from lower depreciation and interest costs.
Much of the initial rebound came from commodity producers, but analysts now expect uninspiring growth across all three major sectors, with cautious assumptions on demand, commodity prices and costs.
Balance sheets are a bright spot: Net debt across the ASX 200, excluding financials, came in $6bn better than expected, with commodity producers edging towards net cash.
Distributions have been resilient. FY26 dividends beat forecasts by 2.6 per cent and FY27 dividend forecasts have held up despite the earnings downgrade. Twenty-one companies flagged new or expanded buybacks, a record for August, worth a combined $4.4bn, led by CSL, Telstra and Challenger.
UBS equity strategist Richard Schellbach paints an equally sober picture. Analysts downgraded this financial year’s earnings on three companies for every two upgrades. Trading updates showed sales growth slowing to 2.2 per cent since June, down from 3.5 per cent in February.
“Inflation now everywhere,” according to Schellbach, with cost pressures in energy, diesel, transport and wages across almost every sector.
Share prices have reflected that unease. Banks had their worst month since June 2022 as credit growth slowed and housing worries build. Healthcare surged 19.3 per cent – its best month on record.
All this comes as the local market faces a fresh test from interest rates. Hotter-than-expected inflation and household spending data last week led Deutsche Bank, NAB and Citi to predict a restart of interest rate hikes by next month. CBA, NAB and Goldman Sachs think the Reserve Bank will wait until November.
Morgan Stanley equity strategist Chris Nicol said the market has been too comfortable.
“The common pushback to our generally more cautious views linked to an equity investor belief that the next move in rates would be down,” he said. He points to “clear evidence from this results season of cost push pressure” as a warning sign.
“A need to hike by the RBA is not in the current market make-up,” he warned. AMP’s Mousina agrees the risk has grown. “Domestic profit growth can’t compete with blockbuster US outcomes and there were more signs (last) week that another RBA rate hike may come sooner than expected,” she said.
A September rate rise is also “clearly a risk”.
Adding to the pressure, US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh gave a hawkish speech at the Jackson Hole symposium on Friday, telling central bankers the Fed “must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed”.
Summer data, he said, “do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved”.
US traders are now pricing a nearly 60 per cent chance of a September Fed hike, with 1.5 hikes priced by year end and more than two by mid-2027 – reviving concerns US rates may stay higher for longer just as the AI boom keeps powering Wall Street.
Futures pricing suggests the ASX 200 will open down about 0.4 per cent near 9056 points on Monday, extending a run of nervous trade.
For local investors, it’s a familiar message – profits are growing again, balance sheets are strong, and dividends keep flowing. But the recovery remains narrow, cost pressures are widespread, and rate risk on both sides of the Pacific is back.
